extracted.intended_audience: editors, proofreaders, compositors, authors, and printers (esp. University of Chicago Press)
extracted.subtask_description: A manual of typographical and editorial rules governing composition, capitalization, italics, quotations, punctuation, divisions, footnotes, indexing, tabular work, technical terms, and related matters for University of Chicago Press publications and similar editorial offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose and application of the Manual
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manual codifies typographical rules employed by the University of Chicago Press; rules are meant for the average case and applied with elasticity; exceptions may legitimately be made for subject-matter, argument emphasis, author preference, or typographical contingency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations are not inviolable—decide exceptions on merits; deference to author's expressed wishes except where taste or logic matters; local conditions and types of publication may call for modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Proper nouns and derived adjectives (Rule 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns (e.g., George, America, Englishman; Elizabethan, French).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names: to boycott, to fletcherize, to christianize, to pasteurize. See also cross-references (e.g., rule 53).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Epithets used as substitutes or affixed to a name (Rule 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize epithets used as substitutes for proper names or affixed to a name (e.g., the Pretender; Richard the Lion-hearted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat epithets forming part of a title or commonly recognized label as capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Particles in French names (Rule 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize particles in French names (le, la, de, du) when standing without a Christian name or title preceding; do not capitalize when preceded by such name or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Bossu, La Torre, De Coligny vs. Rene le Bossu, Miguel de la Torre. Always capitalize 'Van' in Dutch names; never capitalize 'von' in German names (Stephen Van Rensselaer; Hugo von Martins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Generic geographic terms forming part of names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic terms that form part of geographic names (Atlantic Ocean, Mississippi River, Mount of Olives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such words when they are merely descriptive additions (the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara). Lists of generic terms and rules for singular/plural placement are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Adjectives/nouns distinguishing definite regions or groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize adjectives and nouns used singly or together to distinguish definite regions or parts of the world or groups of states (Old World, Western Hemisphere, North, the Orient, Gulf states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not, as a rule, capitalize adjectives derived from such names or nouns designating direction: oriental customs, northern Europe (exceptions noted, e.g., 'Northman').

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Generic political division terms when integral to name
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) Capitalize political division terms when they are organic parts of a name following the proper name directly (Holy Roman Empire, United Kingdom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See subrules (2)-(4) for 'of' constructions, single accepted designations (the States), and fanciful/popular appellations used as names (Eternal City).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: 'Of' constructions used integrally (Rule 2 under 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize terms when used with 'of' as integral part of name to indicate certain minor administrative subdivisions: Department of the Lakes, Town of Lake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization where the term is part of the official name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Single accepted designations (Rule 3 under 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize when a term is used singly as the accepted designation for a specific division (the Union, the States, the Republic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize commonly recognized single-word names for political entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Fanciful or popular appellations (Rule 4 under 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words that form part of fanciful or popular appellations used as if they were real geographical names (Celestial Empire, Badger State).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such popularized names as proper nouns when functioning as names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Numbered political divisions (Rule 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinals and similar terms when designating numbered political divisions: Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 100 for further cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Names of thoroughfares, parks, buildings, etc. (Rule 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of streets, parks, squares, blocks, buildings, etc.: Drexel Avenue, Lincoln Park, White House, Masonic Temple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general designations like 'courthouse,' 'post-office,' 'library' unless used with the place name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Names of political parties, denominations, schools, and adherents (Rule 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of political parties, religious denominations/sects, philosophical, literary, artistic schools and their adherents (Republican, Catholic, Epicurean, Romantic movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize when used in their general sense of spirit or tendency (republican form of government, socialism as an economic panacea). See exceptions and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Names of monastic orders and members (Rule 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of monastic orders and their members (Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formal order names as proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Official titles of organizations and institutions (Rule 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the proper (official) titles of social, religious, educational, political, commercial, and industrial organizations and institutions (Union League Club, Smithsonian Institution, State University of Iowa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic class designations or when standing alone unless to avoid ambiguity or where a word substitutes clearly for the true name (the Hall [Tammany]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Names of legislative, judiciary, administrative bodies and departments (Rule 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of legislative, judiciary, and administrative bodies and governmental departments when specifically applied (Congress, Parliament, Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general or paraphrastic references (the national assembly, the department, the board).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Ordinals for dynasties, sessions, regiments (Rule 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinals used to designate Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, names of regiments, and similar connections (the Eighteenth Dynasty; the Fifty-third Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization where the ordinal is part of the formal designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Historical epochs, language periods, geological ages (Rule 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize commonly accepted appellations for historical epochs, literary/language periods, and geological ages (Crusades, Renaissance, Middle Ages, Pleistocene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'age' is capitalized only where failure to do so would create ambiguity (Stone age vs. Middle Ages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Names for important events (Rule 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize commonly accepted names for important events (Thirty Years' War, Revolution (French), War of 1812, Battle of Gettysburg, Louisiana Purchase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat historically titled events as proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Political alliances and historically significant partisan/group names (Rule 16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize political alliances and historically associated class/movement names that function as party designations (Protestant League, Holy Alliance, the Roses, Independents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization when the term identifies an historical party or movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Conventions, congresses, expositions (Rule 17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of conventions, congresses, expositions, etc. (Council of Nicaea, Fifteenth International Congress of Criminology, Chicago World's Fair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formal conference/exposition titles as proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Titles of treaties, acts, laws, and juridical instruments (Rule 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, bills, and legal instruments (Treaty of Verdun, Art. V of the Peace of Prague, Magna Charta, Fourteenth Amendment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize 'the Constitution' when referring to U.S. Constitution standing alone; otherwise use lowercase for generic references (the constitution of Illinois).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Creeds and confessions of faith (Rule 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of creeds and confessions: Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Augsburg Confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note adjective forms (ante-Nicene) and cross-references for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Civic and ecclesiastical feast-days (Rule 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of civic and ecclesiastical feast-days (Fourth of July, Labor Day, Easter, Passover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the generic 'sabbath' = day of rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Titles preceding or following names and titles of honor (Rule 21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles (civil and military) preceding the name and academic degrees in abbreviated form following the name; capitalize titles of honor and nobility when referring to specific persons (Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Timothy Dwight, D.D.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize titles when following the name (McKinley, president of the United States), when standing alone except in certain exceptions, or when preceded by the article 'the' (the emperor of Germany) — see rule 49 for university specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of acquired, limited, or special-meaning words (Rule 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words that have an acquired, limited, or special meaning (the Doctor's degree; a Bachelor's hood; a Freshman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic forms (the doctorate, a master in chancery when explanatory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize personified abstract terms (Rule 26)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Nature' and similar abstract ideas when personified ("Nature wields her scepter").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization to signal personification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'Father' and 'Reformers' in specific contexts (Rule 27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Father' for church fathers and 'Reformers' for Reformation leaders when ambiguity would otherwise occur (the Fathers, the Reformers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize in generic descriptions (the church reformers of the fifteenth century).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'church' in properly cited titles and edifice names (Rule 28)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Church' in names of nationally organized bodies or when part of the name of a particular edifice (Church of Rome, Fifth Avenue Baptist Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone or in unspecific references (the church, the Roman Catholic church) except in exceptional emphasis cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Names for the Bible and other sacred books (Rule 29)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and titles for the Bible and sacred books (Scriptures, Holy Writ, Koran, Vedas, Apocrypha).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns (biblical, scriptural, koranic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Versions of the Bible (Rule 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of Bible versions (King James's Version, Authorized Version, Revised Version, Septuagint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations like A.V., R.V., LXX are used; treat version names as proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Books and divisions of sacred texts (Rule 31)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize book and division names in the Bible and sacred books (Old Testament, Exodus, Psalms, Gospel of Luke, Epistle to the Romans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic words like 'book,' 'gospel,' 'epistle' when used generically (the five books of Moses, the gospels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Biblical parables and related personages (Rules 32-33)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of biblical parables and certain biblical personages/events (the parable of the Prodigal Son; Last Supper; Eucharist; the Passion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat well-known named items as proper nouns; use lowercase for generic or descriptive uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: First word of a sentence and poetry lines (Rule 34)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and, in poetry, the first word of each line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Greek and Latin poetry, capitalize only first word of a paragraph, not each line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: First word after a colon in specific cases (Rule 35)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when introducing a complete passage or sentence of independent meaning, or where the colon has the force of 'as follows', 'namely', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the first word of a quotation immediately connected with preceding text or where the colon introduces a dependent explanatory phrase; examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: First word in enumerated sections (Rule 36)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, capitalize the first word of enumeration links if any link contains two or more distinct clauses separated by semicolon, colon, or period, unless all are dependent on the same preceding term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate when to capitalize enumerated items depending on clause independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Nouns followed by numerals indicating sequence (Rule 37)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns followed by a numeral indicating order (Room 16, Act I, Vol. I, No. 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize minor subdivisions of publications written in abbreviated form (sec. 4, scene i, art. iii). See cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: First word of a cited speech in direct discourse (Rule 38)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a cited speech or thought in direct discourse whether preceded by a colon or comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show use with quotation marks and without.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: First words in resolutions (Rule 39)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' in resolutions (Whereas, It has pleased God...; Resolved, That...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal legislative/resolution capitalization conventions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: The exclamations 'O' and 'Oh' (Rule 40)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the exclamations 'O' and 'Oh' when used in direct address or exclamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O Lord!' 'Oh, that I were home again!'. See rule 117 for further context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Principal words in English titles and heads (Rule 41)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all principal words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, first and last words) in English titles of publications and their divisions, subjects of lectures, and certain heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cap-and-small-cap and italic center-heads where possible; botanical/generic bibliography exceptions exist (Botanical Gazette style). See rules 172 and 280 for side-heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Foreign titles general rules (Rule 42)
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign titles, capitalize according to language conventions: (a) Latin: proper nouns and derived adjectives; (b) French/Italian/Spanish/Scandinavian: capitalize proper nouns but not derived adjectives; (c) German/Danish: capitalize all nouns; (d) Dutch: capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are provided for each language illustrating the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Definite article in newspaper/magazine titles (Rule 43)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title when mentioning newspapers and magazines (the Chicago Tribune, the School Review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lowercase 'the' outside of formal title usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Titles of ancient manuscripts (Rule 44)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts (Codex Bernensis, Cod. Canonicianus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat manuscript titles as proper nouns; abbreviations MS/MSS used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Nouns in hyphenated title main words (Rule 45)
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds (Twentieth-Century Progress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize hyphenated components that are not nouns (Fifty-first Street; Lives of Well-known Authors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Scientific (Latin) taxonomic names (Rule 46)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize scientific Latin names of divisions, orders, families, and genera (Cotylosauria, Felidae) but not their English derivatives (cotylosaurs, felids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names of species may be capitalized if derived from person names or generic names in botanical/zoological matter; in geological and medical matter, species names are never capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Names and epithets of peoples, races, tribes (Rule 47)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes (Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples listed; use with sensitivity in modern contexts (this is historical guidance in 1906–1911 Manual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: Astronomical body names (Rule 48)
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical work, capitalize names of bodies of the solar system except common terms 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' 'stars' (the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow astronomical naming conventions for proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: University of Chicago administrative divisions and titles (Rule 49)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in official work (the University, the School of Education, the Department of Anthropology, the Board of Trustees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lowercase when speaking generically (the division, the department, the scholarship) except to avoid ambiguity or in official contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Capitals and Small Capitals for dates and salutations (Rule 50)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set town and state in the date line and salutatory/signature phrases of letters in capitals and small capitals (Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911; My dear Mr. Smith:; Charles W. Scott).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting guidance: alignment, indentation, and type size preferences (set to right, indented, and preferably in smaller type).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set Small Capitals for certain words like 'a.m.' 'p.m.' 'B.C.' (Rule 52)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set 'a.m.' and 'p.m.' and 'B.C.' and 'A.D.' in small capitals without space between letters: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small capitals and no internal spaces for these conventional abbreviations; see cross-references to other rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small/lower-case initial letter for commonized former proper names (Rule 53)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial letters for words of common usage originally proper names or their derivatives whose origin has become obscured (utopia, bohemian, titan ic, china (as leathers), boycott).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also applies to verbs derived from proper names (italicize, christianize).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-case minor subdivisions in literary references (Rule 54)
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, use lower-case for minor subdivisions and their abbreviations such as chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note (chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references to numbering rules (37, no., 237).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-case units of measurement (Rule 55)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial letters for units of measurement abbreviations (h. hour, min. minute, sec. second; lb. pound; yd. yard; ft. foot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow conventional abbreviations and lower-case styling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic side-heads capitalization (Rule 56)
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; set the rest in lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for further guidance on side-heads and table heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize first word of quotations connected to preceding text (Rule 57)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a quotation which, through a conjunction or otherwise, is immediately connected with what precedes, even if the original begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 35 and 131 for illustrations and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize for emphasis (Rule 58)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to lend emphasis or importance (e.g., "This was, however, not the case").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italics sparingly for emphasis to signal importance or contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize foreign words and brief foreign passages (Rule 59)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text and not incorporated into English; also single sentences or brief passages from another language not long enough to set in reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung'; 'coup d'etat'; 'par excellence'. Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or foreign institution/place names commonly used in roman type (Pere Lagrange; Reichstag). Do not italicize widely anglicized foreign words (ennui, entree, per cent).
